claims.text: The initial compositionally complex alloy can be a homogeneous, single-phase refractory HEA with a disordered BCC or FCC matrix.
Chemical complexity suppresses conventional grain-boundary segregation in the initial HEA.
Prolonged high-temperature exposure or stress can trigger short-range ordering in an initially single-phase HEA.
Short-range ordering leads to nucleation and gradual coalescence of a brittle Laves or B2 intermetallic phase.
The ordered intermetallic phase nucleates within grain interiors rather than through significant grain-boundary segregation.
Ordered domains grow from the nanoscale to the microscale and eventually interconnect within the ductile matrix.
Above a percolation threshold, the interconnected ordered phase disrupts continuity of the ductile matrix.
Interconnected ordered regions provide preferential crack-propagation paths and thereby degrade toughness.
Service-relevant thermal or mechanical loading can promote ordering while avoiding significant grain-boundary segregation and other degradation mechanisms.
A lower-temperature control condition will prevent ordering and preserve the single-phase state.
Aged or exposed specimens will contain ordered matrix precipitates detectable by TEM or XRD.
Exposure-induced ordering will shift fracture from ductile or mixed behavior toward intergranular or cleavage-dominated fracture.
The exposed alloy will have lower fracture strain and toughness than the initial single-phase baseline.
Formation of the ordered phase may retain or increase yield strength through precipitation hardening despite reducing toughness.
The initial baseline has no detectable secondary phase.
